sets.title: Law and method changes
sets.what: Changes since 2016 that break year-to-year comparisons.
rows: SB 90 (ch. 2021-11): one vote-by-mail request now covers elections only 'through the end of the calendar year of the next regularly scheduled general election' (was two general-election cycles). Standing requests from 2020 expired at the end of 2022; requests made for 2024 expired at the end of 2024, so every 2026 mail voter had to re-request.
Mail requests and mail ballots in 2026 are NOT like-for-like with 2016, 2018 or 2020 (multi-cycle standing requests). 2022 and 2024 share the one-cycle rule. A mail decline vs 2020 is partly law.
SB 7050 (ch. 2023-120) amended s. 101.62 again (request rules and identification fields). The one-request-per-cycle limit is in force for 2024 and 2026.
Same rule in 2024 and 2026; the round-1 claim that SB 7050 created the lapse is wrong: the lapse dates from SB 90 (2021).
V (history line) / I (scope of the 2023 change)
Mail-ballot requests require the voter's Florida driver license number, state ID number or last four of SSN (written requests also signed).
Secure ballot intake stations: at the supervisor's main office, permanent branch offices and each early voting site, staffed/monitored, available during early voting hours (SB 90).
Mandatory early voting: 10th to 3rd day before the election (2026: Sat Oct 24 to Sat Oct 31); counties may add the 15th-11th and 2nd days (Oct 19-23, Nov 1). 8-12 hours per day.
Same statutory window in 2018-2024. 2026 data through Oct 23 include only counties that opened optional days early: many small counties show zero early votes until Oct 24.
Mail ballots must be received by 7 p.m. Election Day (overseas exception s. 101.6952(5)).
Signature-defect cure affidavit accepted until 5 p.m. on the 2nd day after the election.

Canvassing boards may begin canvassing mail ballots after public testing of tabulators; no result may be released before polls close. Florida reports early and mail results first, within minutes of 7 p.m. (ET)/8 p.m. (CT, Panhandle).
Mail and early votes appear first; the Election Day vote (R-leaning in 2022 and 2024) arrives later on election night.
County returns due to the Department of State by noon on the 13th day after the general (Nov 16, 2026).
New congressional map enacted for 2026 (signed 2026-05-04 per the race registry relay). Every FL CD number denotes a different territory than in 2022/2024.
BREAK: no FL CD-level comparison with 2022 or 2024 is valid without re-aggregating precincts to the 2026 lines; the site's FL CD early vote (votingtrend.com) is 2026-only and must say so.

sets.title: Ballot measures
rows: Florida Changes to Budget Stabilization Fund Amendment

Amend the state constitution to increase the amount of funds that may be retained in the budget stabilization fund from 10% to 25% of net general revenue, require an annual transfer to the fund equal to $750 million or 25% of the general revenue collections (whichever is lesser), and allow for the legislature to suspend the transfer under certain conditions.[50]
R (revision-pinned Wikipedia table; measure text not opened at the SOS)
Florida Exempt Tangible Personal Property Used for Agriculture or Agritourism from Property Taxes Amendment

Amend the state constitution to exempt tangible personal property, such as farm equipment or tools, from property taxes if the property is typically present on agricultural land, used for farming or agritourism activities, and owned by the landowner or leaseholder of the land.[51]
R (revision-pinned Wikipedia table; measure text not opened at the SOS)
Florida Amendment 3, Homestead Tax Exemptions, Property Assessments, and Spending Restrictions Amendment

Increase the homestead tax exemption for non-school taxes to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, with the amount indexed to inflation starting in 2029; provide that new residents receive a smaller exemption until they've lived in the state for five years; decrease the cap on how much the assessed value of non-homestead properties, such as rentals and commercial buildings, can increase each year from 10% to 5%, except for school district taxes; limit how counties and municipalities can spend property tax revenue on public safety, education, infrastructure, natural resource projects and flood control, local bonds, employee retirement benefits, and government operations; and other changes.[52]
